vignette.name: VOID Shared Memory
vignette.p: VOID Shared Memory is a low-level, deterministic system for real-time numeric data exchange between independent applications running on the same machine.
It is designed as a shared state space based on POSIX shared memory and a strict, versioned memory contract.
The core idea behind VOID Shared Memory is simple and explicit:

ul.li: one application writes structured numeric data into shared memory
one or more applications read snapshots of that data

vignette.p: The shared memory segment is identified by name and follows a strict binary layout. Writers own structure. Readers consume state.
All shared memory segments follow the VOID Shared Memory Contract, currently version 2.
Each segment starts with a fixed-size binary header containing:

ul.li: a magic number and version identifier

vignette.p: The payload immediately follows the header and consists of 32-bit floating point values organized as:
channels × length
Two counters define the temporal semantics of the system.
The epoch represents a structural generation of the shared memory. Any structural change (such as channels, length, or name) triggers a hard reset of the segment and increments the epoch.
The frame represents activity within a stable structure. Each successful write increments the frame counter.
Readers and observers can reliably detect:

ul.li: activity or stalling via frame progression

vignette.p: Connection is explicit and opt-in on both sides.

ul.li: readers explicitly attach to shared memory

vignette.p: No implicit connections occur. This prevents accidental writers, duplicate publishers, and unintended memory conflicts.
Readers operate in strict snapshot mode.

No persistent pointer to the payload is kept across reads. This guarantees consistency and avoids race conditions.
VOID Shared Memory always represents data using the same fundamental structural model:
channels × length
This model is invariant across all writers and readers. What changes between objects is only how data is projected into that structure.
Regardless of the source or destination object, the shared memory payload is always interpreted as a two-dimensional numeric space:

ul.li: length defines samples or elements per lane (columns)

vignette.p: This consistency allows different object types to interoperate without ambiguity, even when their native representations differ.
Audio-rate writers that operate on signals write one scalar value per channel at each update.
For example, writing a multichannel signal with five channels produces the following shared memory layout:
channels = 5, length = 1
From a matrix-based perspective, this corresponds to a column vector of five values.
No special case exists here: a single-sample signal is simply a length of one.
Matrix-based writers write full blocks of data in one operation.
In this case:

ul.li: the number of matrix rows maps to channels
the number of matrix columns maps to length

vignette.p: The shared memory layout directly reflects the matrix dimensions, without reordering or padding.
Readers always consume the same underlying structure but may expose it using different native representations.
For example:

ul.li: a signal-based reader exposes each channel as a signal
a matrix-based reader exposes the payload as a 2D matrix
a message-based reader exposes the payload as lists or scalars

vignette.p: These are not different data formats, but different views of the same shared memory structure.
To avoid confusion, it is useful to keep a single mental model:

p.i: VOID Shared Memory does not convert data types — it only exposes different projections of the same channels × length structure.

vignette.p: Once this model is understood, moving between signals, matrices, and messages becomes straightforward and predictable.
VOID Shared Memory provides dedicated tools for inspection and supervision without touching payload data.
This enables robust orchestration of complex multi-process systems.
The system supports one-writer, many-reader topologies.
Multiple readers may attach concurrently without coordination. Multiple writers to the same segment are explicitly disallowed by design.
VOID Shared Memory is connector-agnostic.
Any environment capable of POSIX shared memory access and binary struct interpretation can act as a writer or reader.
Current connectors include audio-visual environments and graphical dataflow systems, where shared memory channels naturally map to signal lanes or parameter arrays.
Other connectors can be implemented without modifying the contract.
VOID Shared Memory is intentionally boring at the lowest level, so higher-level systems can be expressive, experimental, and reliable.
